newsitem.title: GERMANY: Large EU malting barley crop points to exports.
newsitem.headline: Large EU malting barley crop points to exports.

text.p: A huge European malting barley crop this year should discourage imports and raise export hopes to third countries, brokers and analysts said on Tuesday.
"Prices have dropped in recent weeks under harvest pressure but there won't be a free fall," one analyst said.
"Although domestic consumption should only be steady, farmers would resist a price collapse by storing the grain."
"Meanwhile, traders would lobby the EU to support sales to the world market by granting export subsidies."
German malt and barley broker Jochen Mautner GmbH in Duesseldorf said some 30-40 percent of Europe's spring barley crop will qualify for malting purposes this year.
He put the spring barley crop in 11 key EU malting barley producing countries at 26.41 million tonnes, up from 19.07 million last year, from a 6.03 million hectare area (5.67 million in 1995).
Spring rain and temperature patterns had been just the right mix to produce big grains and low proteins below 11.5 percent -- the desirable combination for malting.
The area rise was due to replantings after a harsh winter killed rapeseed and barley crops in North Europe. Farmers aimed for malting barley in the hope of premiums over feed barley.
Spain's giant barley area of 2.32 million ha would bring good malting quality after beneficial rain, Mautner said.

Yields were more than double those last year at 3.35 tonnes per hectare and theoretical malting barley availability could be 700,000-800,000 tonnes, around 10 percent of the overall barley crop, after 185,000 tonnes in 1995.
But Mautner said weak transport links would prevent this volume from reaching markets abroad -- apart from truck and rail shipments to France -- and qualities were not overly good.
France expects to achieve 2.2 million tonnes of malting barley from larger and better-yielding winter and spring crops.
With domestic consumption at around 1.5 million tonnes, traders were looking for export channels to replace Germany, which last year took 500,000 tonnes but now looks comfortable.
Mautner said Germany might only import 200,000-300,000 tonnes in the 1996/97 season, roughly a third of its normal import requirements because its barley crop would be ample.
At least 60 percent of spring barley output of four million tonnes this year in Germany should qualify for malting.
Consumption of malting barley at around 2.0-2.5 million tonnes was unlikely to shift either way because beer output and exports were mostly stagnant.
Germany, which normally sold surplus tonnages to France and Belgium, would look to eastern Europe, which was facing poor crop prospects from winter damage and was likely to import.
Here, as well as in other third countries such as China, Germany would compete with EU neighbours, Australia and Canada.
Exporter Denmark was expecting a 3.28 million tonne spring barley crop (up from 2.75 million in 1995), of which 40 percent should be of malting quality, Mautner data showed.
Britain normally exports to Europe but sources were worried a crop they described as "fantastic" would not find its way to Continental markets because of the local competition.
Prices were already more than 10 stg down from a year ago with 138.10 stg a tonne last quoted for U.K. malting barley.
German farmgate prices have fallen to 285-300 marks a tonne versus 320 marks agreed in pre-harvest fixed contracts.
Delivered prices are 35-50 marks higher when transport and malting costs are added.
